title: The Emperor Who Drew the Line: Italica, the Wall, the Nile, and the Drum on the Tiber
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: Italica and the Ward of Trajan

stops.name: Rome: the birth of Publius Aelius Hadrianus
stops.date_confidence: Day attested by the Historia Augusta, which dates the birth to the seventh consulship of Vespasian and the fifth of Titus. The place is disputed: the biographer says Rome, most modern accounts say Italica in Baetica, and no source locates the house, so the pin is a neutral point on the Palatine and Forum ground.
stops.campa: On the ninth day before the Kalends of February a son is born to Publius Aelius Hadrianus Afer, senator, and to Domitia Paulina of Gades. The family is Italican, planted in Baetica since the wars against Carthage, and the boy is cousin to a soldier named Trajan. His biographer says he is born at Rome. Later tradition puts the birth at Italica in Spain, and the two accounts are never reconciled by anyone in antiquity. He will spend more of his life outside Italy than in it, and the argument over which city may claim the first day suits him.
suggested_refs: Historia Augusta, Vita Hadriani 1.1-1.3, the consular dating of the birth

stops.name: Italica: the ward of Trajan
stops.date_confidence: The Historia Augusta says he was deprived of his father in his tenth year, which allows 85 or 86; the sources are not more precise. The death of his mother Domitia Paulina is not dated by any ancient source, and the popular claim that both parents died together is not evidence.
stops.campa: In his tenth year the boy loses his father. The Historia Augusta says that and no more, and says nothing of his mother's death at any date, so the full orphan of the popular account is a half orphan in the evidence. Guardianship passes jointly to two men: his cousin Publius Aelius Traianus, of praetorian rank and rising fast, and the Roman knight Publius Acilius Attianus. One of them will make him emperor thirty-two years from now. The other will kill four senators on his behalf in the first summer of the reign.
suggested_refs: The excavated town of Italica at Santiponce, home ground of the Aelii and the Ulpii

stops.name: Italica: recalled from the hunting
stops.date_confidence: Historia Augusta 2.1 gives 'in his fifteenth year he returned to his native place', which puts the return at about 90; the Roman schooling therefore falls between about 85 and 90.
stops.campa: In his fifteenth year he comes home to Italica, takes up arms, and takes up hunting with such appetite that Trajan calls him off the field. Between the guardianship and this return lies his Roman schooling, where a devotion to Greek letters earns him the name Graeculus, the Greekling, given in mockery by men who will one day watch him finish a temple in Athens that the Athenians could not finish in six hundred years. He hunts for the rest of his life. A city in Mysia is later called Hadrianutherae, Hadrian's hunts, though the boar that tradition has him kill to found it appears in no ancient source.
suggested_refs: Historia Augusta, Vita Hadriani 2.1, the recall from the chase

stops.name: The middle Danube: tribune of Legio II Adiutrix
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction. The tribunate is attested, the year is standard in the modern cursus, but the legion's station in 95 is not fixed. The usual Aquincum pin is anachronistic: II Adiutrix does not garrison Aquincum until about 106, and Pannonia Inferior does not exist until Trajan divides the province in 103.
stops.campa: His first commission is a military tribunate with Legio II Adiutrix on the Danube. Where the legion stands in this year is not fixed in any source: it will not garrison Aquincum until about 106, and the province men later call Pannonia Inferior does not exist until Trajan divides Pannonia in 103. So the pin sits in the middle Danube country near Sirmium and holds the fact rather than the address. He learns the frontier here as a junior officer of nineteen. He will spend the whole of his reign walking it.
suggested_refs: The cursus honorum of Hadrian as reconstructed from Historia Augusta 2.2 and the inscriptions

stops.name: Mogontiacum: the news out of Rome
stops.date_confidence: Nerva adopted Trajan in the autumn of 97, and the congratulatory embassy belongs to that moment; the second ride, carrying news of Nerva's death, falls in January 98. The tribunate in XXII Primigenia at Mainz is 97-98, not the 'c. 95' sometimes printed.
stops.campa: Transferred to Legio XXII Primigenia at Mogontiacum on the Rhine, Hadrian is in Upper Germany in the autumn when word comes that the childless emperor Nerva has adopted Trajan. The army of the province chooses Hadrian to carry its congratulations to his own guardian. In January the old emperor dies, and Hadrian rides again, on foot for part of it after his carriage is sabotaged, ahead of a rival messenger sent by his brother-in-law Servianus, to tell Trajan he is emperor of Rome. He is twenty-one and he has learned what a fast horse is worth.
suggested_refs: The legionary fortress of Mogontiacum, base of XXII Primigenia

stops.name: Rome: Vibia Sabina and the keeper of the records
stops.date_confidence: The marriage is dated to about 100 and the quaestorship to 101 by the Historia Augusta and the standard modern chronology; neither carries a day.
stops.campa: Trajan's wife Plotina arranges a marriage between Hadrian and Vibia Sabina, grand-niece of the emperor, tying the young officer to the reigning house by blood as well as by guardianship. The Historia Augusta says Trajan himself was not enthusiastic. The following year Hadrian is elected quaestor and made keeper of the Senate's records, reading the emperor's speeches aloud to the house in a provincial accent that makes senators laugh at him. He studies until he can speak without giving them the pleasure a second time.
suggested_refs: Historia Augusta, Vita Hadriani 3.1, the quaestorship and the accent

stops.name: Sarmizegetusa Regia: the Dacian wars
stops.date_confidence: Two wars, 101-102 and 105-106, both with Hadrian in the emperor's company. The tribunate of the plebs falls in 105, which belongs to the second war and not, as it is often printed, to the first.
stops.campa: Twice Trajan crosses the Danube against Decebalus, in 101 and again in 105, and both times Hadrian rides with him. He holds the tribunate of the plebs in 105, the opening year of the second war, and takes Legio I Minervia into the field. Trajan gives him a diamond that Nerva had given Trajan, and the court reads the stone as a promise. The Dacian capital burns in the mountains. Its gold pays for a forum in Rome, a column, and a bridge over the Danube, and Dacia is the one Trajanic conquest Hadrian will keep when he hands the eastern provinces back.
suggested_refs: The burnt sanctuary terraces of Sarmizegetusa Regia in the Orastie mountains

stops.name: Aquincum: governor of Lower Pannonia
stops.date_confidence: Attested. The province is four years old at this point, created by Trajan's division of Pannonia in 103; the consulship follows in 108.
stops.campa: Trajan gives him Pannonia Inferior, a province four years old, cut out when Pannonia was divided in 103, with its legionary base at Aquincum on the Danube. The Sarmatian Iazyges raid across the river. Hadrian beats them and then negotiates a peace, which is the sequence he will prefer for the rest of his life and the one his critics will call cowardice. The consulship follows in 108. He is thirty-one, governing a frontier province in his own name, and the men around Trajan have begun to count him among the possible heirs.
suggested_refs: The civil town and legionary fortress of Aquincum in modern Obuda

stops.name: Athens: archon of the city
stops.date_confidence: Attested by the Athenian archon lists and standard modern accounts; no month.
stops.campa: The Greek world he was mocked for loving makes him a citizen of Athens and then elects him eponymous archon, its highest civic magistracy, held by a Roman who is not yet emperor and does not need the office. He wears the archon's dress in the agora where the students of Plato argued and where Aristotle walked out each morning to his own school across the town. This is an honour Athens gives rather than one Rome imposes. Athens will get it back with interest: a temple, a library, an arch, and a league of Greek cities with itself at the head.
suggested_refs: The Athenian archon list for 112/113, naming Hadrian eponymous
sources: Anthony Birley, Hadrian: The Restless Emperor

stops.name: Selinus in Cilicia: the death of Trajan
stops.date_confidence: The death is attested to 8 August 117. The adoption document is the disputed thing, not the date: Cassius Dio holds that Plotina concealed the death and produced the adoption, and the Historia Augusta reports the doubt without settling it.
stops.campa: Sick and turned back from the Parthian front, Trajan dies at Selinus on the Cilician shore, a small harbour town that will be renamed Traianopolis for it. Two days earlier a document is signed adopting Hadrian as son and heir. Whether Trajan signed it is disputed in antiquity itself: Cassius Dio holds that the empress Plotina concealed the death for a few days and produced the adoption, and even the Historia Augusta, which is friendly, reports the doubt without settling it. The pin marks a deathbed no witness agrees on.
suggested_refs: The site of Selinus, later Traianopolis, near modern Gazipasa

stops.name: Antioch on the Orontes: proclaimed emperor
stops.date_confidence: Attested. The governorship of Syria is 117 only: before that Hadrian held no provincial command during the Parthian war and travelled in Trajan's entourage, so the '114-117 as governor' sometimes printed is wrong.
stops.campa: Hadrian is at Antioch, holding Syria with an independent command given him only that year, when the sitting legate was sent to Dacia. On the eleventh of August the eastern army acclaims him emperor and the Senate in Rome ratifies what it cannot refuse. His first act of policy is a subtraction: Trajan's new provinces beyond the Euphrates and the Tigris are given up, Mesopotamia and Armenia abandoned, the frontier drawn back to a line that can be held with the troops that exist. Alexander marched the other way through this country and never came home from it.
stops.quote_source: Historia Augusta, Life of Hadrian 17.1, Loeb Classical Library, trans. David Magie, via LacusCurtius; said on becoming emperor to a man he had counted a personal enemy
suggested_refs: Historia Augusta, Vita Hadriani 5, the abandonment of the eastern conquests

stops.name: Rome: the entry and the four senators
stops.date_confidence: The entry is dated 9 July 118. The executions belong to 118 and are placed before the entry; Hadrian's denial of responsibility and the charge against Attianus are both reported, and neither is verifiable.
stops.campa: He enters his capital in July, nearly a year after the acclamation, and buys the city's goodwill at once: a donative to the people and the soldiers, and the arrears of debt owed to the treasury burned in a heap in Trajan's forum. Before he arrives, four consular senators are dead. Lusius Quietus, Palma, Celsus and Nigrinus are executed on the prefect Attianus's authority for a conspiracy Hadrian swears he never ordered. The Senate believes what it chooses. Twenty years from now it will remember these four and refuse him his godhead.
stops.quote: I have already refused this to your father.
stops.quote_source: Historia Augusta, Life of Hadrian 20.8, Loeb Classical Library, trans. David Magie, via LacusCurtius; said to a grey-haired petitioner who dyed his hair and asked again
suggested_refs: The burning of the debt records in the Forum of Trajan, 118

stops.name: Nemausus: the basilica for Plotina
stops.date_confidence: The tour begins in 121 and the basilica is attested by the Historia Augusta; the month is not recorded.
stops.campa: The first great journey begins. He goes north through Gaul, and at Nemausus he orders a basilica raised in honour of Plotina, dead the year before, the woman on whom his accession rests whether she forged the adoption or witnessed it. The building is a monument and an argument at the same time. Behind him the palace stands empty for years together. Ahead of him lie the Rhine, the Ocean, Britain, Spain, Mauretania, Asia, Greece, Egypt, and every frontier army in the empire, which he intends to inspect with his own eyes.
suggested_refs: Historia Augusta, Vita Hadriani 12.2, the basilica of Plotina at Nemausus

stops.name: Mogontiacum: the frontier closed in timber and earth
stops.date_confidence: The German leg of the tour is 121; the month is a reconstruction from the itinerary, not from a source.
stops.campa: He comes back to the Rhine as emperor, to the fortress where he was a tribune of twenty-one. He tightens the discipline of the German armies: no baths in the daytime, no ornament on the marching kit, the emperor eating camp bread and bacon and cheese in the open with the men and walking twenty miles in armour to prove it can be done. Along the river the frontier is closed with a running palisade of split oak on an earth bank, a line drawn where no river or mountain draws one. Stone comes later. The idea is already whole here.
suggested_refs: The Upper German limes, first palisade phase under Hadrian

stops.name: Pons Aelius: the bridge that takes his name
stops.date_confidence: The British visit is 122. The Legio IX Hispana story is a correction of a popular legend: officers and stamped tiles place the Ninth at Nijmegen on the Lower Rhine after about 120, so it was transferred, not annihilated in Britain; its ultimate fate is unknown.
stops.campa: He crosses the Ocean to Britain with the new governor Aulus Platorius Nepos and the Sixth Legion, brought over when the Ninth Hispana leaves the island. Where the road crosses the Tyne he throws a bridge and gives it his own family name, Pons Aelius, the bridge of the Aelii. The Ninth does not vanish into a northern mist, whatever the story says: its officers and its stamped tiles turn up at Nijmegen on the Lower Rhine after about 120. Where the legion ends after that, no source records, and the gap is a gap.
stops.quote: I don't want to be a Florus, / Stroll about among the taverns, / Lurk about among the cook-shops / And endure the round fat insects.
stops.quote_source: Historia Augusta, Life of Hadrian 16.3-16.4, Loeb Classical Library, trans. David Magie, via LacusCurtius; Hadrian's reply to Annius Florus, whose teasing verses had him strolling about among the Britons
suggested_refs: RIB 1340, the Pons Aelius inscription at Newcastle upon Tyne
sources: Anthony Birley, Hadrian: The Restless Emperor

stops.name: Hadrian's Wall: the line between the seas
stops.date_confidence: Attested to the British visit of 122; construction runs for years after. The pin is the atlas's existing Hadrian's Wall coordinate, inherited from Constantine's Pictish campaign of 306.
stops.campa: From the Tyne to the Solway he orders a wall built across the neck of Britain, eighty Roman miles of it, with a ditch in front, a road behind, mile-castles, turrets, and forts set into the line. His biographer gives the purpose in a single clause: to separate the Romans from the barbarians. It is the plainest statement any Roman emperor makes about a limit. Constantine will campaign north of this wall in 306 and be proclaimed emperor at York within months, on ground Hadrian had already decided was the edge of the world worth holding.
stops.quote: to separate the Romans from the barbarians
suggested_refs: The curtain wall, vallum and mile-castle system between Wallsend and Bowness

stops.name: Tarraco: the winter and the mad slave
stops.date_confidence: The winter of 122/123, spent in Spain; the day is not recorded, and the assassination story rests on the Historia Augusta alone.
stops.campa: He winters in Spain at Tarraco and pays out of his own purse to restore the Temple of Augustus there, calling a council of the Spanish provinces which then refuses him the levies he asks for. In the garden of the villa a slave runs at him with a sword. Hadrian holds the man himself until the attendants come up, then hands him to the doctors rather than the executioner, having judged him mad and not treasonous. The story comes from the same biographer, in the same book, who records the four dead consulars of 118.
stops.quote: Do not walk between those whose slave you may some day be.
stops.quote_source: Historia Augusta, Life of Hadrian 21.3, Loeb Classical Library, trans. David Magie, via LacusCurtius; relayed with a box on the ear to a slave seen walking between two senators
suggested_refs: The provincial forum and Temple of Augustus at Tarraco

segments.name: The Eastern Circuit and the Greek Return

stops.name: Samosata on the Euphrates: the meeting with Osroes
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction as to place. The Historia Augusta says only that Hadrian conferred with Osroes 'on the Euphrates' and names no city; Samosata is conjecture, and the ancient site now lies under the water of the Ataturk reservoir.
stops.campa: Word of a Parthian mobilization takes him east at speed by way of Mauretania and Cyrene. He meets the Great King Osroes on the Euphrates and settles the quarrel in conversation: the king's captured daughter goes home, the golden throne Trajan carried off is promised back, and Parthamaspates, Rome's failed candidate for Parthia, is given Osrhoene to rule instead. No ancient source names the meeting place. The pin at Samosata is a guess, and the town it marks is now under a reservoir.
suggested_refs: Historia Augusta, Vita Hadriani 12.8 and 13.8, the conference on the Euphrates

stops.name: Claudiopolis: the boy from Bithynia
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction throughout. No ancient source records where or when Hadrian met Antinous; Claudiopolis is inferred from the boy's known home town, and 123 or 124 from the emperor's itinerary through Bithynia. The Nicomedia earthquake relief is separately attested by Dio.
stops.campa: Bithynia has been shaken by earthquake, and he pays for the rebuilding of Nicomedia himself, one of dozens of eastern cities he restores and many that take his name in gratitude. Somewhere in this province, in this year or the next, he meets a boy from Claudiopolis called Antinous, thirteen or fourteen years old. No ancient source records the meeting, the place, or the date. Everything about the beginning is reconstruction. Only the end is documented, and even the end is documented three different ways.
suggested_refs: Cassius Dio 69.14 on the rebuilding of Nicomedia after the earthquake

stops.name: Eleusis: the Mysteries
stops.date_confidence: Attested by Cassius Dio; the lower grade in 124 and the higher in 128 is the standard reconstruction, and the Athenian festival calendar puts the rite in September.
stops.campa: At Eleusis, on the bay west of Athens, the emperor of Rome is initiated into the Mysteries of Demeter, taking the lower grade now and coming back four years later for the higher. What happens inside the Telesterion he does not tell anyone, because no initiate tells. Cassius Dio records the fact of the initiation and nothing whatever of its content, which is exactly what the rite requires of him. Hadrian enters as a candidate like any other man, in the month the Athenians appoint, and the empire waits outside the sanctuary wall for its emperor to come out.
suggested_refs: The Telesterion at Eleusis, rebuilt and enlarged under Hadrian and the Antonines

stops.name: Athens: the Olympieion taken up
stops.date_confidence: The Dionysia of March 125 is attested; the Peloponnesian circuit belongs to the winter before, and the constitutional reform to the Athenian stay of 124-125.
stops.campa: He presides at the Dionysia in the archon's dress he wore thirteen years before, and commits the money to finish the temple of Olympian Zeus, begun by the tyrant Peisistratos in the sixth century before Christ and left standing half built by every ruler since. He gives Athens a new civic tribe named Hadrianis and rewrites its constitution. Over the winter he has gone round the Peloponnese paying for temples at Epidaurus, Mantinea, Megara and the Heraion of Argos, restoring the shrines of a country that has been a Roman province for two hundred and forty years.
suggested_refs: The Olympieion of Athens, begun c. 515 BCE and completed under Hadrian

stops.name: Mount Etna: the sunrise from the summit
stops.date_confidence: He is recorded at Dyrrhachium on 20 May 125 and is back in Italy by late summer, so the Sicilian detour falls between; the month is a reconstruction from the itinerary.
stops.campa: Crossing back toward Italy he turns aside into Sicily and climbs Etna in the dark to watch the sun come up from the summit, because he has been told the light at that hour shows the colours of a rainbow. The biographer records it in one line, set between constitutional reforms and frontier policy, as though a Roman emperor climbing a volcano at night to look at a sunrise needed no explaining at all. Nothing in the reign depends on it. He does it anyway, and it is written down.
suggested_refs: Historia Augusta, Vita Hadriani 13.3, the ascent of Etna

stops.name: Rome: the Pantheon and the first villa
stops.date_confidence: The return to Italy is 125, not 126. The Pantheon's brick stamps cluster in 113-125, so the rotunda was begun under Trajan and completed under Hadrian; the villa at Tibur is not finished either, phase one running 118-125 and phase two 125-134.
stops.campa: He is back in Italy by late summer, having been at Dyrrhachium in May. In the Campus Martius stands the rebuilt Pantheon, its rotunda begun under Trajan and finished under him, and it carries on the pediment the name of Agrippa who built the first one, not his own. Out at Tibur the first phase of his villa is done and the second is beginning. Carl Jung will spend a lifetime refusing to come to this city, will faint at the ticket window when he finally books a passage, and will never stand under this dome.
suggested_refs: Brick-stamp dating of the Pantheon rotunda, 113-125

stops.name: Lambaesis: the speech cut into stone
stops.date_confidence: The inspection runs through late June and the surviving adlocutio is dated 1 July 128; the '128-05' sometimes printed is wrong.
stops.campa: He crosses to Africa and inspects Legio III Augusta at Lambaesis in the summer heat, watching the cavalry wheel and the cohorts throw their weapons, and then he addresses the troops. The address is cut into a column standing in the camp and it survives. He praises the drill and corrects the faults, an emperor talking shop with professionals, and every word of it comes down in his own recorded speech instead of a historian's summary. His arrival is credited locally with breaking a five-year drought.
suggested_refs: CIL VIII 2532 = ILS 2487, the Lambaesis adlocutio of 1 July 128

stops.name: Athens: the Panhellenion
stops.date_confidence: The second Eleusinian initiation and the founding work of the Panhellenion belong to the Athenian stay of September 128; the league is formally constituted in 131/132.
stops.campa: Back at Eleusis in September for the higher grade, he sets about the largest of his Greek projects: a league of the Greek cities of the empire, the Panhellenion, with Athens at its head and membership granted on proof of Hellenic descent. Cities from Asia and Cyrene and the Peloponnese send delegations with their genealogies to be judged. It is an antiquarian's empire built inside the real one, and it gives the Greek east a capital that is not Rome, two hundred and eighty years after Rome took Greece's freedom away.
suggested_refs: The Panhellenion inscriptions recording admitted cities and their claims of descent
sources: Anthony Birley, Hadrian: The Restless Emperor

stops.name: Palmyra: the city takes his name
stops.date_confidence: Attested by Palmyrene inscriptions naming the city Hadriane Palmyra; the visit is dated to 129 in the standard itinerary and the month is not recorded.
stops.campa: The caravan city between the desert and the Euphrates receives him, and afterwards calls itself Hadriane Palmyra in its own inscriptions, with the privileges of a free city. Its wealth is other people's goods in transit, silk and pepper and slaves moving between the Parthian world and the Mediterranean one, taxed at the gate by a council of merchants. Hadrian has given up conquering the country the caravans come from. He is content to tax what it sends and to fix the frontier where the road already is.
suggested_refs: Palmyrene and Greek inscriptions naming the city Hadriane Palmyra

stops.name: Gerasa: the arch outside the walls
stops.date_confidence: The winter of 129/130 in the Decapolis; the arch's inscription dates it to the visit.
stops.campa: He winters in the Decapolis, and Gerasa builds him a triumphal arch to come in by, three arches high, set well south of the town on the assumption that the city will grow out to meet it. The city never does grow that far. The arch stands alone in the field for nineteen centuries, a gate into open ground, still carrying the inscription of the year the emperor came. From here he goes down into Judaea with a plan in his baggage that will cost the province, on Cassius Dio's count, more than half a million lives.
suggested_refs: The Arch of Hadrian at Jerash and its dedicatory inscription
sources: Inscription of the Arch of Hadrian, Gerasa

stops.name: Jerusalem: the colony decreed
stops.date_confidence: The visit and the decision are dated 130. The cause of the revolt is contradicted between sources and is left unresolved here: Dio says the founding of the colony provoked it, the Historia Augusta says the ban on circumcision did. The pin is the atlas's canonical Temple Mount coordinate.
stops.campa: He comes to a city still in ruins sixty years after Titus burned it, and decides to refound it as a Roman colony named for his own family and the Capitoline gods, Aelia Capitolina, with a temple of Jupiter standing on the platform where the Temple stood. Solomon built on this rock. Nebuchadnezzar levelled the first house. Jesus taught in the courts of the second. Cassius Dio says the colony is what starts the war; the Historia Augusta says it was the ban on circumcision, and the two accounts are not reconciled.
suggested_refs: The Hadrianic fill and street grid of Aelia Capitolina beneath the Old City

stops.name: Pelusium: the tomb of Pompey
stops.date_confidence: Attested by the Historia Augusta and by Dio, who preserves the verse; no month is given.
stops.campa: At the eastern edge of the Delta he finds the grave of Pompey the Great neglected and half buried, the man who lost the republic's last war and was murdered on this beach as he stepped out of the boat. Hadrian rebuilds the tomb at his own expense and writes the verse for it himself. He is restoring the monument of the losing side of a civil war a hundred and eighty years cold, in the same season in which he has decided to take the name of Judaea off the map, and he goes on south with the whole court behind him.
stops.quote: Strange lack of tomb for one with shrines o'erwhelmed!
stops.quote_source: Cassius Dio, Roman History, Epitome of Book 69, Loeb Classical Library, trans. Earnest Cary, via LacusCurtius
suggested_refs: The site of Pelusium at Tell el-Farama, landing place and grave of Pompey

stops.name: Alexandria: the questions in the Museum
stops.date_confidence: The Egyptian stay runs from summer 130; the month here is a reconstruction from the itinerary. The Museum disputation is Historia Augusta 20.2 and Dio 69.3.1, not HA 14.4 as it is sometimes cited.
stops.campa: In Alexandria he goes to the Museum and puts questions to the professors, then answers the questions himself, which the professors are obliged to endure. The city is the intellectual capital of the Greek world and the granary of Rome, and it argues with its emperors from habit. This season he hunts a lion in the Libyan desert with Antinous beside him, the first firm record of the two of them travelling as a pair, and the poet Pankrates will turn the kill into verse before the year is out and dedicate it to the library the emperor has just interrogated.
suggested_refs: Historia Augusta, Vita Hadriani 20.2, the disputation in the Museum

stops.name: Hermopolis Magna: Antinous in the river
stops.date_confidence: No ancient source dates the drowning. The imperial party kept the Nile festival of Osiris on 22 October 130 and the body was found shortly after, so the event belongs to late October; the '24 October' widely printed is a modern reconstruction, not a datum.
stops.campa: The imperial flotilla is on the Nile for the festival of Osiris, the days in which the god's own drowning in this river is mourned and his rising is celebrated. Antinous goes into the water near Hermopolis and does not come out. Accident, suicide, ritual sacrifice: the ancient accounts offer all three and settle on none, and Hadrian's own lost memoirs said, according to the biographer, only that the boy fell into the Nile. The emperor weeps like a woman, Dio reports, and is mocked in Rome for weeping. No source gives the day.
suggested_refs: The Nile festival of Osiris, 22 October, and the conflicting ancient explanations of the drowning

stops.name: Antinoopolis: the city for the drowned
stops.date_confidence: The foundation date of 30 October 130 is the standard one; the deification and the games are attested by Dio and by the cult material.
stops.campa: On the east bank opposite Hermopolis he founds a Greek city where the body came ashore, names it for the boy, gives it a constitution, games called the Antinoeia, and a cult. He deifies Antinous without consulting the Senate, which is not a thing an emperor does for a private person from Bithynia. The cult takes hold and spreads. It reaches some seventy cities, produces something near two thousand statues within eight years, and is still being suppressed by imperial edict two and a half centuries later, under Theodosius, in 391.
suggested_refs: The plan of Antinoopolis recorded by the Napoleonic Description de l'Egypte before the site was quarried away

stops.name: The Colossi of Memnon: Balbilla's verses
stops.date_confidence: Attested to 20 November 130 by the inscriptions themselves, which date by regnal year and by the Egyptian month of Hathyr.
stops.campa: At Thebes the court goes out before dawn to hear the northern colossus of Amenhotep sing, as the cracked stone does when the first sun warms it. On the first morning it stays silent for the emperor, which is noticed. On the twentieth of November it sounds for the empress, and Julia Balbilla of Sabina's household cuts four poems into the statue's foot and leg in Aeolic Greek, the dialect of Sappho, six hundred years out of date and chosen deliberately. Hadrian's own verses at the same site are lost.
stops.quote: I came here alongside my beautiful queen Sabina, as the sun kept its course in the first hour.
stops.quote_source: Julia Balbilla, verse inscription on the left foot of the Colossus of Memnon, Thebes (IGRR I 1173-1176); translation from sententiaeantiquae.com, translator not credited
suggested_refs: The four Balbilla epigrams on the northern Colossus of Memnon

segments.name: The Last Years and the Tomb

stops.name: Athens: the Olympieion dedicated
stops.date_confidence: The dedication falls in the winter of 131/132, spent in Athens; the day is not recorded.
stops.campa: He winters in Athens a third time and dedicates the finished temple of Olympian Zeus, some six hundred and forty years after Peisistratos laid its foundation course. The Athenians raise an arch beside it that divides the city in two, with Theseus named on the western face and Hadrian on the eastern. In the same season the province of Judaea rises behind him under Simon bar Kokhba, and the second half of the reign turns from building temples to a war the emperor will direct but will not attend in person for long.
suggested_refs: The Arch of Hadrian at Athens and its two inscribed faces

stops.name: Tibur: the villa and the end of travelling
stops.date_confidence: His return to Rome is epigraphically certified on 5 May 134; earlier scholarly guesses run to 132 or 133, and the frequently printed 131 is wrong, since he wintered in Athens in 131/132.
stops.campa: The return to Italy is fixed by inscription to the fifth of May, and he comes back to the villa at Tibur, where the second building phase has raised a canal called the Canopus after the Egyptian town, a shrine to Antinous, and quarters named for the places he has been: the Lyceum, the Academy, the Poikile, the Vale of Tempe, and an underworld called Hades. He has rebuilt the empire in one park at the scale of a garden. He is ill with what looks like heart failure and dropsy, and he does not travel again.
suggested_refs: Historia Augusta, Vita Hadriani 26.5, on the naming of the villa's quarters
sources: Anthony Birley, Hadrian: The Restless Emperor

stops.name: Beitar: the end of the revolt
stops.date_confidence: The fall of Beitar is dated 135 in the standard chronology; no day. Dio's casualty figures are ancient numbers and are reported as such, not endorsed.
stops.campa: Sextus Julius Severus is brought from Britain, the Danube legions are drawn south, and the war is won the slow way, by starving out one strongpoint at a time rather than by battle. The last is Beitar, southwest of Jerusalem, where Bar Kokhba dies. Dio counts fifty fortresses and nine hundred and eighty-five villages destroyed and five hundred and eighty thousand killed. Judaea is renamed Syria Palaestina, Jews are barred from the city, and the crusader Jerusalem that Richard Lionheart fails to take stands on the streets Hadrian lays out here.
suggested_refs: Khirbet el-Yahud at Battir, the siege works of the last rebel fortress

stops.name: Rome: the succession settled
stops.date_confidence: The adoption of Antoninus is 25 February 138. Sabina dies in 136; Lucius Aelius Caesar dies 1 January 138; Servianus and Pedanius Fuscus are executed in 137, not 138.
stops.campa: Sabina dies in 136 after a marriage the biographer calls miserable, and the rumour that Hadrian poisoned her is written down and not proved. He adopts Lucius Ceionius Commodus, who is consumptive and dies on the first of January 138 before he can inherit anything. His brother-in-law Servianus, ninety years old, and Servianus's grandson Pedanius Fuscus are put to death in 137 over the succession. On the twenty-fifth of February he adopts Antoninus, on condition that Antoninus adopt Marcus Annius Verus in turn.
stops.quote: We have leaned against a tottering wall and have wasted the four hundred million sesterces which we gave to the populace and the soldiers on the adoption of Commodus.
stops.quote_source: Historia Augusta, Life of Hadrian 23.14, Loeb Classical Library, trans. David Magie, via LacusCurtius
suggested_refs: Historia Augusta, Vita Hadriani 23-24, the two adoptions

stops.name: Baiae: the little soul
stops.date_confidence: Attested to 10 July 138. Sources differ on whether the villa is described as at Baiae itself or nearby, and the difference is not resolved.
stops.campa: He is dropsical and in constant pain, and he asks for poison and then for a sword, and is refused both by servants and physicians who will not let him die at his own hour. At the villa on the bay he dies on the tenth of July, sixty-two years old, having reigned twenty-one years. Dio gives among his last words the remark that many physicians have killed a king. The biographer gives five lines of Latin addressed to his own departing soul, and they are the only poem by a Roman emperor that the world has kept by heart.
stops.quote: O blithe little soul, thou, flitting away, / Guest and comrade of this my clay, / Whither now goest thou, to what place / Bare and ghastly and without grace? / Nor, as thy wont was, joke and play.
stops.quote_source: Historia Augusta, Life of Hadrian 25.9, Loeb Classical Library, trans. David Magie, verse translation by A. O'Brien-Moore, via LacusCurtius
suggested_refs: The Latin text of the animula poem as printed in the Latin Library edition of the Historia Augusta

stops.name: Puteoli: the villa that had been Cicero's
stops.date_confidence: The burial at Puteoli in the villa Ciceroniana is specified by Historia Augusta 25.7; the month is not recorded. The vaguer 'near Baiae' found in some accounts is imprecise.
stops.campa: Antoninus buries him first at Puteoli, in the estate that had been Cicero's, because the mausoleum in Rome is not finished. The body is then moved to the Gardens of Domitia across the Tiber to wait. The Senate, which remembers the four consulars of 118 and the two dead men of 137, refuses to make him a god. Antoninus tells the house that if Hadrian is not deified then Hadrian's acts are void, including the adoption that made Antoninus emperor. The Senate yields, and calls him Pius for making it yield.
suggested_refs: Historia Augusta, Vita Hadriani 25.7, burial at Puteoli in villa Ciceroniana
sources: Historia Augusta, Life of Antoninus Pius 5.1-5.2

stops.name: Mausoleum of Hadrian: the ashes come home
stops.date_confidence: Completion in 139 is the standard date, a year after the death; the day is not recorded.
stops.campa: The drum of travertine and marble on the far bank of the Tiber is finished the year after his death, with a bridge built on purpose to reach it, and the ashes of Hadrian, of Sabina, and of Lucius Aelius Caesar are placed inside. Every emperor down to Caracalla in 217 will be laid here after them. He designed his own tomb and did not live to see it standing, which is the ordinary condition of tombs. It outlasts the empire that raised it by fifteen hundred years.
stops.quote: animula vagula blandula, / hospes comesque corporis, / quae nunc abibis in loca / pallidula rigida nudula / nec, ut soles, dabis iocos!
stops.quote_source: Historia Augusta, Life of Hadrian 25.9, Latin text as printed by The Latin Library (thelatinlibrary.com/sha/hadr.shtml); punctuation and capitalization vary across editions
suggested_refs: The Pons Aelius, now Ponte Sant'Angelo, built to serve the mausoleum

stops.name: Mausoleum of Hadrian: the urns emptied
stops.date_confidence: The sack of Rome is firmly dated to 24 August 410. The breaking open of the mausoleum and the scattering of the ashes come from later accounts rather than from an eyewitness, and are reconstruction.
stops.campa: Alaric's Goths come in through the Salarian Gate on the twenty-fourth of August and are three days in the city. The mausoleum has been a fortress since about 401, built bodily into the Aurelian walls, and it is broken open: the urns are emptied, the ashes thrown out, and nothing that was placed inside in 139 is known to survive anywhere. The account comes from later writers, not from anyone who was there. The building itself takes no harm from losing its purpose and is a fortress again in the morning.
suggested_refs: The absorption of the mausoleum into the Aurelian Walls, c. 401

stops.name: Castel Sant'Angelo: the archangel on the roof
stops.date_confidence: Legend, recorded in later hagiographic and civic tradition rather than in a sixth-century source. The name it gives the building is the attested part.
stops.campa: Plague is in Rome, and Gregory leads a penitential procession over the bridge, and the archangel Michael is seen on the roof of the tomb sheathing his sword, and the plague stops. That is the legend, written down later, and it gives the building the name it still carries. The popes take it for a citadel and a prison. Charlemagne kneels to a Pope Hadrian at Saint Peter's a few hundred metres upstream in 774, a different Hadrian altogether. Otto III has Crescentius beheaded on this roof in 998.
suggested_refs: The bronze Michael on the summit of Castel Sant'Angelo, successor to earlier figures of the same legend

stops.name: Villa Adriana: the first measured plan
stops.date_confidence: Attested. Ligorio's survey of 1550 is conventionally called the first large-scale archaeological excavation of the modern kind; the earlier papal digs under Alexander VI are dated to about 1500.
stops.campa: Fourteen hundred years of quarrying have carried the villa's marble into other men's buildings and its statues into other men's gardens. Pius II comes out to look at the ruins in the fifteenth century, Alexander VI has them dug about 1500, and in 1550 Pirro Ligorio, architect to Cardinal Ippolito d'Este, surveys the whole site and draws the first measured plan of it. Piranesi draws it in the eighteenth century and his son publishes a second general plan in 1781. UNESCO inscribes the site in 1999.
suggested_refs: Pirro Ligorio's 1550 survey and Francesco Piranesi's 1781 general plan of the villa
sources: Piranesi publication history via academic summaries

stops.name: Chesters on the Wall: the stone bought back
stops.date_confidence: Attested. Camden's visit is 1599 and Clayton begins buying land in 1834; by his death in 1890 he owns five forts and most of a twenty-mile stretch of the Wall.
stops.campa: William Camden rides to the Wall in 1599 and writes the first coherent account of it, reading the Roman line off the open landscape. Two and a half centuries later John Clayton, town clerk of Newcastle, begins buying the land it runs through to stop farmers carting the facing stones away for barns, and ends by owning twenty miles of it and five forts: Chesters, Carrawburgh, Housesteads, Vindolanda, Carvoran. The order to separate the Romans from the barbarians survives because a solicitor bought the fields it crosses.
suggested_refs: Clayton's excavated bath-house and fort at Chesters (Cilurnum), near Chollerford
sources: English Heritage, John Clayton and Chesters Roman Fort
